Business API map: Fresco

What the API lets the business do, who may call it, the journeys that matter and what sits behind them. Business-first, not an endpoint catalog.

Overview

The Fresco API lets a household without an account turn a declared diet and allergy profile into a safe, shoppable week of meals, and lets that same household pay for Pro when it wants the menu to learn from what it actually cooks. A first-time visitor gets a real anonymous Supabase session, saves consent, a profile and a full weekly menu without ever typing an email. The same session can later become a permanent account with the same user id, or, if the email already belongs to someone, hand its generated data to that account after proving ownership (ADR-0003, ADR-0022).

The API is not one service. Business-critical and cross-user operations run as nine Supabase Edge Functions; billing, consent, waitlist, data export, health probes and the auth-email redirect run as Next.js route handlers on Vercel; and per-household state (favorites, ticking a shopping item, swapping two days) goes from the browser straight to Postgres through RPCs and tables guarded by row level security. Menu selection, shopping-list consolidation and the Pro learning explanation are deterministic code. No LLM is called anywhere in production (ADR-0005).

Two business rules shape every journey. First, Free and Pro call the same endpoints with the same bodies; the server reads user_profiles.plan and decides whether the history reads and the soft preferences feed the selector (ADR-0001, ADR-0071). Second, subscription state is never written by the browser: only a Stripe-signed webhook and a daily reconciliation job write it. Read this map in order: who may call, what each group is for, six journeys, the architecture and the gaps.

Permission and auth model

Authorization in Fresco is row ownership through auth.uid(), not roles. The database has no admin column; the only role-like rule is an environment allowlist. Callers reach each tier below with one of five credentials: a Supabase JWT, a Stripe signature, a cron secret, the Supabase secret key on the apikey header, or a service-role key held only by server code.

Not tiers

  • Free, Pro and Family are one principal. generate-meal-plan reads plan and runs the history reads and soft preferences only when isProEntitlementActive() says so: a paid plan whose plan_expires_at has not lapsed, with a 30-day grace after the first failed payment. Model it as a branch on a column, never as a permission.
  • Recent proof of identity. Two destructive calls take a second token: delete-account needs reauthToken and reassign-guest-data needs targetAccessToken; both must be authentic, issued under five minutes ago, and answer one generic 401 for every failure.
  • Bot protection. Cloudflare Turnstile tokens ride on the Auth calls that create or probe accounts. In a production deploy a missing site key is a refusal, not a pass: /api/waitlist and /api/auth/guest-email answer 503 (captchaMissingInProduction). Whether Supabase Auth enforces the captcha server-side is a hosted setting; supabase/config.toml leaves [auth.captcha] commented out.
  • Per-user throttles are a counter in Postgres (check_and_increment_rate_limit, ADR-0010), fail closed, with a registered endpoint list. Limits per hour: generate-meal-plan 5, update-recipe-status 60, generate-shopping-list 60, get-shopping-list-suggestions 120, reassign-guest-data 5, delete-account 5, checkout 10, portal 20, export 10, guest email change 3 per guest plus 10 per IP. An exemption table for test accounts exists (rate_limit_exempt_users); the data map records it as emptied.

Token flow

A client signs in with Supabase Auth and receives a JWT plus refresh token held by @supabase/ssr. On every page request proxy.ts calls getSession(), which reads the cookie locally and goes to Auth only when the access token is inside the refresh margin, and rewrites the cookie. Edge Function calls carry Authorization: Bearer; the function builds a request-scoped client with that header, calls auth.getUser() and either continues with RLS applied as that user or answers 401. A 401 seen by lib/api/edge-functions.ts sends the browser to /login?session_expired=1; a transient Auth failure is a 503 so the person is not logged out for an outage (FRESCO-1250).

Journey: upgrade to Pro

Business purpose: self-serve subscription, monthly or annual, with a 7-day card-less trial once per account. Revenue critical, so every step is built to refuse before it charges and to heal if a confirmation is lost.

  1. The upgrade dialog first records the withdrawal waiver with POST /api/consents. The route stamps the server's legal-text version and writes through the service-role RPC record_consents; with no record the client never calls checkout.
  2. POST /api/stripe/checkout with an optional { interval }. Guards in order: 401 without a session, 403 for a guest, an unconfigured price (500, or 400 for annual), 503 when this deploy's Stripe mode differs from the mode the shared database serves (ADR-0061), 429 over 10 per hour, 409 without a profile, 409 when already Pro, 400 without a waiver recorded in the last 30 minutes, 409 when Stripe shows a live subscription.
  3. The guards read Postgres: the billing state of the profile, the waiver in user_consents, billing_mode and the rate-limit counter.
  4. The route ensures a Stripe customer (created up front, keyed on the user), then creates a subscription Checkout Session with client_reference_id set to the user id, a session that expires in about 30 minutes, an idempotency key shared by concurrent calls of the same minute, and Spanish locale. The 7-day trial with payment_method_collection: if_required applies only when the profile holds no Stripe customer or subscription id; otherwise a card is required. A subscription in payment trouble (unpaid, paused, incomplete) sends the person to the Billing Portal instead of opening a second checkout.
  5. The response is { url } and the browser navigates there.
  6. The person pays on Stripe's hosted page and returns to /profile?checkout=success. Nothing on the return path writes the plan.
  7. Stripe posts a signed event to POST /api/stripe/webhook. The raw body is verified (400 on a bad signature or missing secret). The six handled types are checkout.session.completed, checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded, customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted, charge.refunded and charge.dispute.created; any other type is a 200 no-op. The event's livemode must equal this deploy's key mode and the database's billing_mode or the answer is 400.
  8. The handler claims event.id in stripe_webhook_events: already completed answers 200 without re-running, claimed by a live run answers 409 so Stripe keeps retrying, an expired claim is retaken, an unrecordable claim answers 500.
  9. For a grant, grantProFromCheckoutSession retrieves the subscription from Stripe. Updated and deleted events also decide from the live subscription, so a late event cannot undo a newer state (ADR-0062).
  10. With the service role it writes plan, the Stripe ids, plan_expires_at and the Stripe mode on user_profiles. A handler error releases the claim and still answers 200, except a transient Stripe or database failure, which answers 500 so Stripe retries.
  11. The profile page re-reads user_profiles.plan and shows Pro.

Recovery and unwinding

  • Lost webhook: GET /api/cron/stripe-reconcile runs daily at 04:17 UTC. It first sweeps paid Checkout Sessions of the last 48 hours whose user lacks that subscription, then re-derives state for each subscribed profile (five at a time, 40 seconds budget), then downgrades orphans, retries pending confirmation emails and writes a heartbeat. It refuses to act when the key's Stripe mode differs from billing_mode.
  • Full refund: charge.refunded cancels the subscription it paid for; the resulting deleted event downgrades. Chargeback: charge.dispute.created cancels it and is reported to Sentry. Both events must be subscribed in each Stripe webhook endpoint, an owner action.
  • Failed payment: past_due stamps payment_failed_at once and keeps Pro; unpaid downgrades. The entitlement check caps the grace at 30 days.
  • Why only the server writes the plan: a database trigger refuses subscription-column changes from any client role, so a compromised browser cannot grant itself Pro (ADR-0007). The two writers are the webhook and the reconcile job.

Endpoints involved: POST /api/consents; GET /api/stripe/pro-price; POST /api/stripe/checkout; POST /api/stripe/portal; POST /api/stripe/webhook; GET /api/cron/stripe-reconcile.

Entities touched: user_profiles (subscription columns), user_consents, stripe_webhook_events, billing_mode, pending_confirmation_emails: business-data-context sections entity-user-profiles, flow-pro-subscription, flow-stripe-reconciliation, state-user-profiles, state-stripe-webhook-events, flow-consents

Journey: guest becomes an account

Business purpose: convert a guest who liked the first menu into a permanent account without losing it, and never let the conversion path become a way to mail strangers or take over someone else's account. Security critical.

  1. The browser posts the typed email and a Turnstile token to POST /api/auth/guest-email. The route requires a guest session (401 without, 403 for a registered user), validates the address, refuses a production build with no site key (503), verifies the token with Cloudflare (400 invalid, 503 when it cannot be verified) and spends 3 attempts per hour per guest.
  2. With the service role it checks 10 attempts per hour per IP and calls grant_guest_email_change, which inserts a one-shot grant that expires in 60 seconds. A trigger on auth.users refuses any write of a pending email for an anonymous user without a live grant, so calling Auth's own update endpoint directly cannot bypass the captcha and the limits (20261103180000).
  3. The route calls auth.updateUser({ email }); Auth mails a code to the new address and the Auth error, if any, is passed through with its status and code.
  4. Email free: the route answers { ok: true } and the screen asks for the code.
  5. The browser verifies the code with verifyOtp of type email_change.
  6. It sets the password with updateUser, adding current_password when the session came from a password sign-in. The user id never changes, so her menu stays where it is.
  7. Email taken (email_exists): the browser signs in to the existing account on a throwaway in-memory client and keeps the resulting access token, leaving the guest session live.
  8. POST reassign-guest-data with the guest JWT and { targetAccessToken }. The function requires a guest (400 otherwise), spends 5 per hour, and refuses the target token unless it is authentic, belongs to a registered account (400), differs from the guest and was issued under five minutes ago (generic 401).
  9. Verification of the target token is a plain auth.getUser() with that token, so brute force happens against Auth's own protections, not against this function (ADR-0022).
  10. With the service role, reassign_guest_data(from, to) moves menus and shopping lists, skips weeks the target already has, and re-filters the moved plans against the target's allergen profile, retiring any slot that conflicts.
  11. The orphaned anonymous user is deleted with auth.admin.deleteUser; a failure here is logged and does not undo the move.
  12. The answer is { reassigned: true, slots_quitados }, so the person learns how many dishes were taken out for food safety, and the client switches to the target session.

Endpoints involved: POST /api/auth/guest-email; POST /reassign-guest-data; Supabase Auth: verifyOtp, updateUser, signInWithPassword.

Entities touched: auth.users, meal_plans, meal_plan_recipes, shopping_lists, user_profiles, guest_email_change_grants: business-data-context sections flow-guest-conversion, access-control, entity-operational-tables

Features: business-feature-context section module-auth-guest (FEAT-004, FEAT-126)

Journey: delete the account

Business purpose: a person can leave for good without being billed afterwards and without leaving personal data behind. A billing failure holds the deletion back; an analytics failure does not (GDPR art. 17). Irreversible, so the sequence proves identity first and ends billing before it erases anything.

  1. A registered user signs in again immediately before the call. A guest has no password and skips this step.
  2. Auth returns a fresh access token.
  3. POST delete-account with the session JWT and, for a registered user, reauthToken. The function throttles 5 per hour and rejects an authentic token that is not hers, not under five minutes old, or missing, with one generic 401.
  4. It validates the re-auth token with auth.getUser() on a client built from it.
  5. Stripe first: it reads stripe_customer_id with the service role; a registered user without one is looked up in Stripe through her checkout sessions, because the webhook may not have written the id yet. It refuses to touch Stripe with a key of the wrong mode, then cancels immediately and refunds the unused period. Any Stripe failure answers 502 and the account is NOT deleted. When a refund is impossible (already refunded, disputed, older than the refund window) deletion proceeds and the owner refunds by hand (ADR-0043).
  6. Only then does auth.admin.deleteUser remove the user, and ON DELETE CASCADE removes every table she owns.
  7. The person is erased in PostHog. If that fails the account is already gone: the outcome is recorded in account_erasures and the daily 04:30 UTC job retry-posthog-erasures retries up to 10 times per row inside a 110 second budget, then keeps the row and logs it.
  8. The answer is { deleted: true }. No plan column is written; the webhook stays their only writer.

Endpoints involved: POST /delete-account; retry-posthog-erasures (no browser caller); Supabase Auth sign-in.

Entities touched: auth.users with its cascade, user_profiles, account_erasures: business-data-context sections flow-account-deletion, entity-operational-tables

Features: business-feature-context section module-profile and module-observability (FEAT-011, FEAT-112)

Journey: first menu without an account

Business purpose: show a visitor a full week of safe meals before asking for anything. It is the whole premise of guest mode (PRD journey 1) and the place where a food-safety defect would be a health incident, not a UX bug.

  1. The identity step signs the visitor in anonymously, after she ticks the age, terms and privacy boxes; a retry reuses an existing session instead of burning another anonymous sign-in. Turnstile rides on this call when configured.
  2. Auth returns a JWT for a real user with is_anonymous = true.
  3. The browser posts the accepted kinds to POST /api/consents; the server stamps the current legal-text version. No consent on record, no progress.
  4. The route writes the rows through the service-role RPC record_consents; clients hold no INSERT grant on user_consents.
  5. The wizard upserts user_profiles directly, under RLS. A trigger refuses allergens or diet flags without a health_data consent, which is why step 3 comes first.
  6. POST generate-meal-plan with { semana_iso, fecha_inicio }. A malformed body is a 400 that does not spend the 5 per hour limit; then 404 without a profile, 409 when the week already has a plan.
  7. get_filtered_recipes(user) removes, in SQL, every recipe that conflicts with her allergens, diet or disliked ingredients. It is the single structural food-safety gate; fewer than 21 survivors is a 422 and no degraded menu is ever generated.
  8. The recipes come back; selection then runs in process and is deterministic: the seed is the user id plus the ISO week, so the same user and week yield the same menu. A slot with no safe candidate becomes a sentinel plus a warning, never a hard failure.
  9. The function calls the service-role RPC create_meal_plan, which writes the plan and up to 21 slots in one transaction. Errors map to 400 (invalid week), 403 (104 saved plans), 409 (concurrent request for the same week), 500.
  10. The response is the enriched menu plus any warnings; the client goes to /menu.

Endpoints involved: POST /api/consents; POST /generate-meal-plan; Supabase Auth signInAnonymously; direct user_profiles upsert and RPC get_filtered_recipes.

Entities touched: auth.users, user_profiles, user_consents, recipes, meal_plans, meal_plan_recipes: business-data-context sections flow-guest-onboarding, flow-menu-generation, flow-consents

Features: business-feature-context sections module-auth-guest, module-onboarding, module-menu-generation, module-food-safety

Journey: cooking marks and the Pro learning read

Business purpose: the one mechanism Pro is sold on. Everyone records what they cooked or discarded; only Pro and Family accounts get the next menu shaped by it. It is also the highest-blast-radius authorization check, because the write feeds counters every Pro generation reads.

  1. The user marks a slot cooked or discarded: POST update-recipe-status with { meal_plan_recipe_id, estado }. The function throttles 60 per hour, whitelists estado (400) and requires nueva_recipe_id for a substitution.
  2. It loads the slot together with its plan's owner, using the caller's own JWT.
  3. Postgres returns the slot and owner. The function answers 403 when the owner is not the caller, and 409 when the transition is not allowed: a mark is final except inside the current ISO week, where it can be taken back or switched (FRESCO-1014).
  4. For a substitution the candidate first passes get_filtered_recipes (422 when it carries a declared allergen, breaks the diet or does not exist) and may not duplicate a recipe already in that week (409). Then the service role writes the one slot, filtered on the state it read, so a concurrent change is a 409. The slot table rejects client updates to these columns, and the database learning trigger records the first cook or discard per user and recipe.
  5. The answer is { ok: true, estado }.
  6. Next week the client calls generate-meal-plan as in the first-menu journey.
  7. Only when isProEntitlementActive is true does the function read the last two weeks of marks and the all-time engagement through two auth.uid()-bound RPCs. Cooked recipes may repeat, discarded ones never come back, and the personal counts nudge the score. Favourite cuisines, goal and cooking level are Pro-only soft preferences (ADR-0071). A failed history read is reported to Sentry and the plan says it was generated without history.
  8. The plan is persisted exactly as for Free. The Free path never issues the history reads, which is the technical difference between the tiers.
  9. The response carries the learning explanation card for Pro, built deterministically from the same data.

Endpoints involved: POST /update-recipe-status; POST /generate-meal-plan.

Entities touched: meal_plan_recipes (state machine), recipe_user_feedback, recipes counters, user_profiles.plan: business-data-context sections flow-learning-loop, state-meal-plan-recipes, flow-menu-generation

Features: business-feature-context sections module-learning-loop, module-menu-generation

Journey: the shopping list

Business purpose: turn the week's menu into an aisle-ordered, costed list the household can tick off in the shop, and keep it honest when the menu changes.

  1. POST generate-shopping-list with { meal_plan_id, refresh? }, throttled at 60 per hour before any work.
  2. The function reads the plan with her own JWT, so RLS answers 404 for a plan that is not hers, and checks whether a list exists: 409 when it does and refresh is off, 404 when refresh is on and there is none.
  3. It loads the slots and their recipes (404 when none).
  4. Consolidation and aisle classification are deterministic code; no consolidable ingredient is a 422. The cost estimate comes from a static per-unit table in the function, not from any supermarket call. A normal run inserts one shopping_lists row (a concurrent duplicate is a 409); a refresh rebuilds the list in place and merges the user's ticks and additions.
  5. The response is the list with its estimated cost range.
  6. Ticking, adding a suggestion, removing a suggestion and clearing ticks are direct RPCs (jsonb_set_comprado, jsonb_add_item, jsonb_remove_item, jsonb_clear_comprados) under RLS: no orchestration, so no Edge Function.
  7. POST get-shopping-list-suggestions with { shopping_list_id }, 120 per hour.
  8. It reads her favorites and passes them through filter_allowed_recipe_ids, so a suggestion never reintroduces an allergen.
  9. The answer is the list of items worth adding, from real data only.

Endpoints involved: POST /generate-shopping-list; POST /get-shopping-list-suggestions; RPCs jsonb_set_comprado, jsonb_add_item, jsonb_remove_item, jsonb_clear_comprados.

Entities touched: meal_plans, meal_plan_recipes, recipes, shopping_lists, favorites: business-data-context section flow-shopping-list

Features: business-feature-context section module-shopping-list

Local, staging and production use the same project, so a staging test writes production rows
Scheduled workpg_cron inside the database (guest cleanup, rate-limit cleanup, waitlist purge, reconcile, erasure retry, weekly push) and GitHub Actions outside it (uptime and heartbeat monitors, backups, drift checks)Edge Functions, route handlers, job_heartbeatGET /api/health/jobs answers 503 when a heartbeat is stale, and an hourly workflow opens an issue; five jobs write a heartbeat, the rate-limit cleanup does not

There is no API gateway or load-balancer configuration. Deploys are independent: one Vercel deployment for the app and supabase functions deploy for the functions.

External integrations at the API boundary

Configuration is by variable name only: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_PRICE_ID_PRO_MONTH, STRIPE_PRICE_ID_PRO_ANUAL, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET_DEV/_PRE/_PROD, CRON_SECRET, TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY, RESEND_API_KEY, GMAIL_SMTP_APP_PASSWORD, VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY/VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY/VAPID_SUBJECT, SENTRY_DSN, POSTHOG_API_KEY, ADMIN_USER_ID.

There is no external LLM or model endpoint (ADR-0005).

Cross-references

  • Data entities this API touches (bun run context:map business-data-context --section <id>): entity-user-profiles, entity-meal-plan-recipes, entity-shopping-lists, entity-user-consents, entity-operational-tables, entity-supermarket-layer, access-control, automatic-processes, and the flows flow-guest-onboarding, flow-menu-generation, flow-learning-loop, flow-shopping-list, flow-guest-conversion, flow-pro-subscription, flow-stripe-reconciliation, flow-account-deletion, flow-consents, flow-waitlist, flow-weekly-push.
  • Features this API backs (bun run context:map business-feature-context --section <id>): module-auth-guest, module-onboarding, module-menu-generation, module-learning-loop, module-shopping-list, module-billing, module-profile, module-food-safety, module-admin, module-observability, and route-inventory for the literal endpoint list.
  • Contract source: there is no OpenAPI spec and no api/openapi.json. The prose contract is .context/SRS/api-contracts.md (written before most of the hardening in this map) and the request and response types under api/schemas/. The route handlers and Edge Function entry files are the authority.
  • Supabase-direct domains: they have no spec and no schema types of their own; the generated database types in lib/supabase/types.ts are the contract, and they lag the migrations (see gaps).
  • Downstream consumers: project-context master-plan mode sequences API-backed work from this map, and sprint-development reads the relevant journey before scoping a story that touches menu generation, marks, the shopping list or Stripe.

Discovery gaps

What could not be verified or looks unfinished. Each item says what to run or read next.

  1. Not run, not queried. The app was not started, no hosted endpoint was called and the hosted database was not queried; every statement comes from the code and migrations at commit a7938eb8. Whether the hosted project matches the repo, including which Edge Functions are deployed and which migrations are applied, is checked by bun scripts/check-functions-drift.ts and supabase migration list --linked, and the drift workflows.
  2. Hosted Auth settings are not visible in code. supabase/config.toml has [auth.captcha] commented out, so whether the hosted project enforces Turnstile on Auth calls, and the real anonymous sign-in and email send limits, cannot be read from the repo.
  3. Vault and secret population is unverifiable from code: the Vault secrets the cron migrations read, CRON_SECRET in the Vercel Production scope, the VAPID secrets and the Stripe webhook secrets per environment. A missing one makes the job answer 401 or 500 and shows up only through /api/health/jobs or Sentry.
  4. Stripe dashboard state is not discoverable: which events each webhook endpoint is subscribed to (charge.dispute.created is an owner action, scripts/check-stripe-go-live.ts checks it at go-live), the configured prices and their tax behavior, and the dunning setting.
  5. No OpenAPI spec exists, so request and response shapes are not mapped here and .context/SRS/api-contracts.md is older than this map. Where they disagree, trust the code.
  6. The feature map is about a month behind the code (dated 2026-10-30) and the data map 2026-10-29. Both were read through the reader and were consistent with the code for every claim used here, but later changes (for example FRESCO-1250 transient Auth failures as 503, and FRESCO-1226 and 1227 soft preferences) are in this map and not in them.
  7. Journey cap: six journeys are traced, under the default cap of seven, chosen by revenue (Pro checkout), security (guest conversion, account deletion) and core value (first menu, learning loop, shopping list). Not traced as journeys: the weekly push (summarized in architecture and integrations), the supermarket price layer, the waitlist double opt-in, data export and the consent re-prompt. Each recombines calls already traced or has no app caller.
  8. The supermarket price RPCs get_supermarket_prices and get_supermarket_demand exist and are exercised only by database tests and the manual refresh script; no code under app/, components/ or lib/api/ calls the read RPC, so shoppers see no price from that layer. Shopping-list costs come from the static table in generate-shopping-list/aisle-pricing.ts. The PRD describes supermarket links and an estimated cost; that behavior was not traced here.
  9. update-recipe-status still accepts estado = sustituida with a safety re-check, but no screen was found that issues it (the calendar swaps with swap_meal_plan_slots, and ingredient substitution is a separate RPC). Possibly dead or planned.
  10. Email reaches real customers only through the Gmail SMTP switch. Resend sends from onboarding@resend.dev and delivers to the account owner only, until a domain is verified (FRESCO-886); without GMAIL_SMTP_APP_PASSWORD in an environment the subscription and waitlist emails do not reach customers there. Supabase Auth mail depends on the Gmail sender and its daily cap (ADR-0021).
  11. One Supabase project serves local, staging and production. Any staging or local API call writes production data, and the Stripe mode guard (ADR-0061) exists because of it. Deliberate, so every other write path compounds the risk.
  12. No heartbeat covers the rate-limit cleanup job, and the heartbeat of the Stripe job records a pass that reached its end, not that every profile was reconciled.
  13. Edge Function CORS is a hardcoded list of three origins; adding an environment means editing _shared/cors.ts and redeploying every function.
  14. Row-level policy and grant claims in auth-model come from the data map and the migrations, not from the live database: access-control says its grants were read from migrations, and this pass did not re-query them.
  15. Legal texts are provisional and the founder accepted the risk (ADR-0066); the consent version stamped by POST /api/consents is therefore a provisional one.
  16. The legacy markdown map (.context/business/business-api-map.md, last updated 2026-10-14) was read as input and is not deleted. Its sections on the supermarket layer, the scheduled-jobs table of GitHub Actions and the Mercadona dataset were not migrated; the data map covers them.
